editorNote: Summer CES puts complete home-computer systems—not bare specifications—at the center of the sales pitch.
morningLine: Chicago’s summer electronics show belongs to a game maker’s ambitious new computer.

lead.headline: Coleco’s $600 Adam Steals the Summer CES
lead.dek: A complete computer, word processor, fast tape drive and letter-quality printer promises to turn a ColecoVision household into a home office.
body: The busiest conversation at Chicago’s June 5–8 Consumer Electronics Show begins with an unlikely challenger. Coleco, best known for ColecoVision, has unveiled Adam: an under-$600 home-computer package built around a Z80 processor, a full-size 75-key keyboard, SmartWriter word processing, BASIC, a Digital Data Pack recorder and a daisy-wheel printer.

That bundle is the point. Buyers accustomed to pricing a computer, storage unit, software and printer separately are being shown the whole desk at once. Coleco says existing ColecoVision cartridges will work, includes Buck Rogers: Planet of Zoom, and promises an expansion route below $400 for current console owners.

Inside, Coleco describes 80K of total memory and an “Adamnet” communications circuit coordinating the system’s processors. The proprietary tape promises far faster transfers than an ordinary cassette, while the printer is rated near ten characters per second. Additional drives are projected at $150 and tapes around $10.

The applause comes with an important reservation: these are show prototypes, not production machines available for a full test. Delivery, reliability and the real retail price will determine whether Adam becomes a family computer or merely the most memorable promise of CES.

Still, Coleco has changed the argument for the week. Atari and Commodore now face a rival selling a complete activity—writing, printing, programming and playing—rather than asking shoppers to assemble a system one peripheral at a time.
lead.confidence: Exact-week announcement; specifications and prices are period claims for prototype hardware.

stories.headline: Atari Answers With XL Computers and a Writing System
stories.dek: The 600XL and 800XL lead a refreshed line, while a $600 bundle makes word processing the competitive measure.
body: Atari’s June 5 announcement brings new computers, peripherals, video accessories and 28 games to the same Chicago floor. The 600XL and 800XL are positioned as successors to the 400 and 800, retaining the value of Atari’s existing software library while offering a cleaner route into the next generation.

Its $600 Writing System combines a 600XL, AtariWriter cartridge, guide, paper and a letter-quality printer rated at 20 characters per second. A television and cassette or disk storage remain extra, but Atari argues that separately useful components give owners more freedom to expand than an all-in-one package.
stories.confidence: Exact-week product announcement with period follow-up coverage.

stories.headline: Software Price War Breaks Out at CES
stories.dek: Cross-platform publishing and sharp price cuts make low-cost computers more useful.
body: The hardware contest is spilling onto the software shelves. Creative Computing reports Datamost Gentry programs for Apple and Atari at $14.95–$19.95, Synapse Showcase titles for VIC-20 at $19.95, and TI-99/4A cassette programs below $10.

Commodore announces 70 titles, Easy Script 64 below $50 and Multiplan for the Commodore 64 at a quoted price that falls toward $50 during the show. Atari, Mattel, Imagic, Activision, Parker Brothers, Broderbund and Sega are all widening platform support as publishers chase the expanding installed base.
stories.confidence: Same-week CES reporting published in a period magazine.

stories.headline: WarGames Makes the Home Modem a Movie Star
stories.dek: A teen, an acoustic coupler and a military computer carry dial-up culture into packed theaters.
body: WarGames enters its second weekend just as home computers dominate the CES conversation. Matthew Broderick plays David Lightman, whose password guessing and modem exploration reach a military system and turn an innocent search for games into a nuclear crisis.

The film ranks fifth for June 10–12 with $4.8 million from 843 theaters and $14.2 million cumulative. Its thriller machinery makes passwords, dial-up exploration and connected systems understandable—and alarming—to audiences far beyond the computer club.
